questions.q: What does a Cosmos DB primary or secondary account key actually grant?
options: Full read-write (or read-only) access to every database and container in the account, with no per-container scoping
Read-only access to a single container the key was created for
Access only to metadata, never to data itself
Nothing — keys are only used for billing, not access
questions.explain: Account keys are account-wide bearer tokens — there's no concept of a key scoped to just one container or database.

questions.q: Why is embedding a Cosmos DB account key directly in a mobile or client-side web app a real risk?
options: The key can be extracted by decompiling the app or found in source control, and whoever holds it has full account access
Client apps cannot technically use account keys at all, so this would simply fail
It's not actually a risk as long as the app uses HTTPS
Account keys expire automatically after 24 hours, limiting exposure
questions.explain: Keys are bearer tokens — the same risk as hardcoding a SQL Server sa connection string into a mobile app.

questions.q: What does Azure AD / RBAC-based access provide that account keys don't?
options: Identity-based access tied to a managed identity or Azure AD user, centrally auditable and revocable without rotating a shared secret
Faster query performance than key-based authentication
Automatic encryption of data at rest that keys don't provide
The ability to bypass network firewall rules entirely
questions.explain: RBAC ties access to an identity Microsoft can centrally manage, audit, and revoke — with a managed identity, there's no secret to leak in the first place.

questions.q: What is the difference between what account keys/RBAC control versus what network isolation controls?
options: Keys/RBAC control who can authenticate; network isolation controls where the connection is allowed to come from at all
They control exactly the same thing and are redundant with each other
Network isolation replaces the need for any authentication
Account keys are a network-layer control, not an identity-layer control
questions.explain: These are two independent, stackable layers — a relational DBA's instinct to combine a login with a firewall rule applies directly here.

questions.q: Which of these is a real network isolation option for Cosmos DB mentioned in this lesson?
options: VNet service endpoints, Private Endpoints, and IP firewall rules
Only account key rotation, since Cosmos DB has no network-layer controls
Disabling Azure AD entirely
Setting the account to 'public read-only' mode
questions.explain: These three are the real network isolation mechanisms available for restricting where Cosmos DB traffic can originate from.
